sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A cold front remains stalled offshore today with mainly dry conditions for interior areas and light rain at times near the coast. A series of frontal systems will bring a return of widespread rain and occasionally windy conditions Friday into early next week.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Saturday night)
paragraphs: A frontal system remains stalled offshore today for another dry and mild day across western WA. Temperatures continue to track warmer than average with highs around 60. East winds will increase across the Cascade tonight with gusts to 20-30 MPH in the gaps and foothills.

The stalled frontal system will slowly track east and inland on Friday with the bulk of the rain along the coast. Rain will spread inland mid to late morning and afternoon with around a tenth to a quarter inch for most areas. High astronomical tide and lower pressure may lead to minor to moderate coastal flooding. The timing would be around the time of high tide Friday morning. In addition, large waves will reach the coast with seas of 20 ft and a High Surf Advisory is in effect.

Another strong Pacific frontal system is poised to impact the Pac NW Saturday-Sunday for more rain, gusty winds and high elevation snow. Rain-wise, we're looking at another 1-3 inches of rain along the coast this weekend with 0.50-1.00 inches in the interior. Additional rainfall in the Olympics will keep the Skokomish River running high with the potential for flooding. It'll be windy too with the potential for strong wind gusts along the coast of 40-50 MPH. Interior areas will see gusts of 30-40 MPH (winds peaking Saturday night). 33

sections.title: Long term (Sunday through Thursday)
paragraphs: Showers will linger on Sunday and Monday with a trough over the region. Snow levels will lower to around 4000 ft on Monday with just light snow amounts in the mountains. Temperatures will track closer to average with lows in the lower 40s and highs in the lower 50s. The next system slated for midweek is pushing south toward Oregon with some wrap-around moisture clipping our southern border. A Rex Block pattern sets up over the West late in the week with drier conditions forecast for western WA. 33

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Generally VFR across western Washington this afternoon with pockets of LIFR conditions in lingering fog through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. A stalled frontal boundary just offshore will maintain periods of MVFR conditions along the coast in rain showers through the early morning hours Friday, with the frontal system and associated rain moving inland Friday morning into the early afternoon. Low level wind shear may impact terminals as the frontal system moves through. Ceilings will likely briefly dip to MVFR as the rain pushes through Friday morning, though conditions are favored to remain predominantly VFR for much of the day. The exception will be along the coast, where IFR conditions are expected to develop by Friday morning and continue throughout the day in rain, low ceilings, and mist. Post frontal showers will develop Friday afternoon, with slight chances for a few lightning strikes along the coast which may impact HQM, but confidence not high enough to include in the TAF at this time. Surface winds will generally remain south/southeast through the period, with winds generally 5-10 kt with gusts to 20 kt for the Puget Sound terminals and higher gusts up to 30 to 40 kt along the coast and over the mountains.

KSEA...VFR conditions with high clouds will continue into the mid morning. A frontal system will push inland between 12z-18z, bringing rain and potential for low level wind shear at the terminal. While conditions are expected to remain predominantly VFR, MVFR may briefly develop in heavier rain showers. Winds will generally remain out of the south or southeast around 10 kt or less, with gusts to 20 kt developing at the terminal Friday afternoon.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Small Craft Advisories for the East Strait of Juan de Fuca and Grays Harbor Bar will continue through the evening as SCAs transition to a Gale Warning over the coastal waters this evening as a stalled frontal system begins to push inland. The strongest winds will occur over the coastal waters later this evening into early Friday morning, reaching high end gale force. An occasional storm force gust cannot be ruled out, particularly over the outer coastal waters. Winds will remain elevated over the coastal waters and over the East Entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca throughout the day Friday, with Small Craft winds picking up over the northern inland waters late Friday as the front shifts eastward.

While winds over the inner waters remain elevated into Saturday morning, winds over the coastal waters will briefly decrease. A Small Craft Advisory has been issued for seas during this lull in wind, with an even stronger frontal system moving in close behind. Ensembles continue to show strong potential for Storm Force winds over the outer waters on Saturday, with an 60% to 70% chance of maximum wind gusts exceeding 50 knots over the outer coastal waters.

Small Craft winds are favored to continue on Sunday, at least over the coastal waters and potentially over some of the inner waters as well. Conditions are favored to calm by Monday, with potential for continued windy conditions over the waters returning by Tuesday.

Seas will remain elevated through the weekend as a series of dynamic systems cross area waters. Friday's system will bring very large seas to the Washington coast, with high confidence in waves building to 20 feet or above by Friday afternoon, with waves across the coastal waters as high as 26-27 feet. These large waves will also be very energetic, with a dominant period of 18 to 22 seconds. Seas will remain elevated through Saturday morning and will briefly ease a bit into early Sunday, remaining between 14 to 18 feet. Another system will send another round of large, long period waves on Sunday with another round of waves likely 20 feet or higher through early Monday. Seas look to ease a bit after Monday, but will likely stay in the 12-15 foot range heading into the middle of next week.

synopsis: A series of frontal storm systems bring will bring periods of high surf and sneaker waves to the coast and rain and breezy conditions areawide through at least early next week. Snow will begin to fall above 4000 ft in the Cascades late Sunday into Monday.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A series of frontal storm systems bring will bring periods of high surf and sneaker waves to the coast and rain and breezy conditions areawide through at least early next week. Snow will begin to fall above 4000 ft in the Cascades late Sunday into Monday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Water vapor satellite imagery shows an upper level pinching and cutting off the southern California coast. Meanwhile, a deep low pressure is spinning over the northeast Pacific and shifting east-southeastward towards the Pacific Northwest. An earlier WPC surface analysis estimated the surface low pressure at 960mb.

Ensembles are in good agreement this strong low pressure will push a front towards the coast late tonight before pushing into the I-5 corridor around daybreak. A strong wind field of 60-70 kt at 925mb will develop off the southern and central coast of Oregon before the front makes landfall. East to west pressure gradient forces should keep most of these winds off the coast, particularly off the north Oregon and south Washington coast.. However, the pressure gradients do open ever so slightly that some of this wind field could be realized at our most exposed locations along the central coast of Oregon. Right now estimating there is a 30% chance that our windiest sites meet High Wind Warning criteria with lower odds north of Tillamook County. As a result, will hold off on any high wind products, but will need to monitor trends and monitor buoy observations to see how well they are tracking with modeled wind fields. Either way, given the pressure gradients the strongest winds are unlikely to last more than 1-2 hours along any portion of the coast, which should reduce impacts. The bigger impact of this storm system will be another round of high surf along the coast late Friday into early Saturday. See the beach hazards section below for more information.

Models and their ensembles are in good agreement an embedded shortwave trough will swing northeastward into the area Friday afternoon into early evening, which should aid in creating a more organized band of showers spreading into the region around that time. Cooler sea surface temperatures near the coast may limit vigorous convection coming onto the coast, but wind fields will be supportive of some rotating storms farther offshore Friday.

The next storm system is currently south of the Aleutian Islands and will shift eastward over the next 48 hours. As it does so, another low pressure will deepen rapidly to around 960mb and move into the place of the current existing low pressure over the northeast Pacific. This will push another front eastward into the region Saturday night bringing another round of increased winds along the coast. It appears there is a 30% chance for a low end High Wind event along the coast late Saturday before a cooler and more showery weather regime takes hold. Snow levels will drop from above 6000 ft early Sunday to near 4000 ft by Monday morning. Given unmaintained mountain roads are free of snow and open, will likely need a Winter Weather product for the Cascades even if only a few inches of snow fall Sunday night into Monday.
There looks to be a brief lull in the wet and breezy weather Tuesday-ish before most global ensemble members suggest another storm system impacts the region around Wednesday of next week. /Neuman

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 18Z Friday...Dry, south to southwest flow aloft will continue through this evening with high level clouds streaming across the area today. As of 18z Thu, dense fog continues to persist across portions of the central and southern Willamette Valley, with LIFR conditions at KSLE and KUAO, as well as near KHIO. Expect the surface inversion to break by 19-20z this morning leading to predominately VFR conditions across the forecast area. There is around a 30-40% chance that IFR fog redevelops after 04z Friday, but an approaching frontal system is expected to bring increasing winds and cloud cover late tonight. Chances for rain also increase at the coast after 08z Friday, spreading inland by 10-12z Fri as a front approaches the region from the west. CIGs are expected to gradually lower with chances for MVFR increasing after 16-18z Friday. South to southeast winds increase along the coast early Friday morning with gusts up to 20-30 kt.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...High clouds continue to stream northward overhead with VFR conditions expected through at least 18z Friday. Light east to southeast winds continue through this evening. Chances for light rain increase after 10-12z Fri as a front approaches the region. Chances for MVFR CIGs also increase to around 20-30% after 17z Fri. /DH

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A stalled frontal boundary offshore will continue to weaken through this morning. Seas of around 12 to 16 ft with a period of 13-15 seconds lingers this morning, maintain marginal hazardous seas across the coastal waters. By this afternoon, southerlies again ramp up ahead of the next low pressure system that will approach the area later Thursday into Friday. A strong Gale Force front is expected to peak early Friday morning, with south to southeasterly winds gusting over 34 kt for potentially over 24 hours. There is also a 40-50% chance for Storm Force wind gusts to occur across the outer coastal waters during the peak timing, but probabilities remain too low to upgrade to a Storm Watch. Therefore, the Gale Watch has been upgraded to a Gale Warning, and is in effect for all coastal marine zones from this evening through Friday afternoon.

Seas are expected to become very steep and hazardous by Friday as a fresh south-southwesterly swell likely develops, building seas to around 14 to 18 ft with a dominant period of around 10-11 seconds. This will be followed by a strong, long-period westerly swell that is expected to build seas above 20 ft Friday afternoon, with a 40-70% chance of seas greater than 25 ft. There is also a 10-30% chance for significant wave heights reaching 30 ft in the outer waters, with highest chances to the south. Another strong front is expected to move across the waters later Saturday into Sunday with high chances for another round of strong southerly Gales, while seas remain elevated through the weekend. ~12/DH

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A tidal anomaly from persistent southerly winds and warmer than average ocean temperatures will result in the total tide pushing 10.5 ft at the Garibaldi tidal gauge Friday afternoon. Historically this typically produces flooding along Fraser- Burton Road south of Tillamook along the Tillamook River. Elsewhere, lowland and agriculture flooding will occur, but it does not appear Highway 101 will be impacted in Pacific County where the Toke Point gauge is anticipated to top out near 11 ft.

More importantly, a large westerly swell will push towards the coast Friday afternoon and peak late Friday evening (most likely between 7-10 PM). This swell will take aim at the southern Oregon coast, but a swell of 25+ ft will still push onto the central and north Oregon coast while the swell will be closer to 20 ft along the south Washington coast. Given periods will be in the 17-19 second range, these waves will have a lot of mass and momentum than the typical Winter time storm swell. This will result in waves running significantly farther up on area beaches and jetties.

Or more simply put, the sneaker wave threat will be extreme. People should use extreme caution as sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning. In addition, large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave.

The large westerly swell will gradually subside Saturday. However, another westerly swell that will be pushing 20+ ft with dominant periods of 16-17 seconds arrives Sunday afternoon and lasts into Monday. This will necessitate another High Surf product and result in another round of high surf conditions, beach erosion and sneaker waves during this time. /Neuman
